subject: Art & Design
title: Brand Naming: The Art of the Perfect Word
description: A quick, practical guide to Brand Naming: The Art of the Perfect Word.

hook.text: Google was almost called BackRub. Nike was almost Blue Ribbon Sports. A name can make or break a brand.

buildup.text: Brand names come in types: descriptive (PayPal), invented (Kodak), metaphorical (Amazon), and founder-based (Ford).

discovery.text: Great names are short, easy to spell, and ownable. They sound like what they mean: Slack feels casual, Uber feels grand.

twist.text: Many iconic names were initially hated. Executives at Sony thought the name sounded too foreign for Japan.

climax.text: Häagen-Dazs is a completely made-up word. It sounds Danish but means nothing. The exotic feel was the whole strategy.

punchline.text: A great brand name doesn't describe the product. It becomes it.

quiz.question: What type of brand name is 'Kodak'?
options: An invented name with no prior meaning
A descriptive name explaining the product
A name derived from the founder's surname

details.summary: Brand names fall into categories: descriptive (General Electric), invented (Kodak, Xerox), metaphorical (Amazon, Apple), founder-named (Ford, Chanel), and acronyms (IBM, BMW).
details.whyItMatters: A brand name is the single most repeated element of identity. A bad name can cripple marketing efforts despite a great product.
takeaways: Names can be descriptive, invented, metaphorical, or founder-based
The best names are memorable, pronounceable, and emotionally resonant
A bad name can cripple marketing despite a great product

faq.question: Why do many tech companies use invented names?
faq.answer: Invented names (Google, Spotify, Zillow) are easier to trademark since they don't exist in any language. They become vessels that the brand fills with meaning over time. They also avoid cultural baggage and translate across languages without unintended associations.

faq.question: How do naming agencies create brand names?
faq.answer: They generate hundreds to thousands of candidates through brainstorming, linguistic analysis, and cultural screening. Names are filtered for trademark availability, domain availability, negative connotations in other languages, and pronunciation across target markets.
